title: Modules and Classes
summary: Modules split code into files. Classes describe how to make objects that share the same kinds of values and actions.
introduction: Modules split code into files. Classes describe how to make objects that share the same kinds of values and actions. A recipe book has separate pages, and one recipe can make many cakes. Learn these two ideas in small, separate steps.
learningObjectives: Export and import values between ES modules and load them with type="module"
Tell named exports from the default export and use each correctly
Define a class with a constructor, methods, private fields, getters and static members

blocks.text: Classic `<script>` files share one global scope: a `const total` in one file collides with a `const total` in another, and nothing tells you which file provides a function. An **ES module** is a file with its own scope. Everything in it is private unless marked with `export`, and anything it needs from another file is declared with `import` at the top. Modules also run in strict mode automatically and are deferred, so they never need the `defer` attribute.

blocks.text: Named exports and the default export

A module can have any number of **named exports**, imported in braces with their exact names (rename with `as`), and at most one **default export**, imported without braces under any name you choose. `import * as math` collects every named export into one object. Paths must be relative (`./` or `../`) or full URLs, and the `.js` extension is required in the browser. `import()` with parentheses loads a module on demand and returns a promise, which is how large apps load rarely used screens only when needed.

blocks.title: Modules need a server
blocks.text: Opening an HTML file that uses `type="module"` straight from disk (a `file://` address) fails in most browsers, because module files are fetched with the same security rules as network requests. Serve the folder with a local server: the Live Server extension in [VS Code](/tutorials/vscode), or `npx serve` if [Node.js](/tutorials/nodejs) is installed.

A module can also be written inline. The page below has a single inline module: it cannot import local files in this sandbox, but it shows module scope, automatic strict mode and top-level `await` in action.

blocks.text: A **class** is a template for objects. The `constructor` runs when you call `new Product(...)` and sets up the new object's properties through `this`. Methods are written like the shorthand methods of an object literal and are shared by every instance. Fields that start with `#` are **private**: only code inside the class can read them, so the object controls how its state changes. A **getter** (`get inStock()`) computes a value that reads like a property, and a **static** method belongs to the class itself rather than to instances, which suits factory functions such as `Product.fromJSON`.

blocks.title: Forgetting new
blocks.text: Calling a class like a function, `const pen = Product("Pen", 2)`, throws `TypeError: Class constructor Product cannot be invoked without 'new'`. The `new` keyword is what creates the object that `this` refers to inside the constructor. Static methods are the exception: `Product.fromJSON(...)` is called on the class itself, and it uses `new` internally.

`class Dog extends Animal` makes `Dog` inherit every method of `Animal`. A subclass can **override** a method by defining one with the same name, and can still reach the parent's version with `super.method()`. In a subclass constructor, `super(...)` must be called before `this` is used, because it is the parent constructor that creates the object. `instanceof` checks the whole chain, so a `Puppy` is also a `Dog` and an `Animal`. Keep hierarchies shallow; two levels are usually enough, and composing objects is often clearer than inheriting.

blocks.text: Inside a method, `this` is the object the method was called on, which is why the same method works for every instance. The link is made at call time, not at definition time: if you take a method off its object (to pass it as a callback, for example) and call it on its own, `this` is `undefined` and the method fails. `bind` creates a copy with `this` fixed, and an arrow function wrapper keeps the call on the object.

items: Use a plain object literal for a one-off bundle of data or settings; it needs no class.
Use a class when many objects share behaviour and keep state that must stay consistent, such as a shopping cart, a timer or a game entity.
Prefer composition (an object that *has* a logger) to deep inheritance (an object that *is* a special kind of logger).
Frameworks such as [Angular](/tutorials/angular) build on classes; [TypeScript](/tutorials/typescript) adds types to the same syntax.

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: Write a `BankAccount` class with a private `#balance`, `deposit` and `withdraw` methods that reject invalid amounts by throwing, a `balance` getter and a static `fromJSON` factory. Then create a `SavingsAccount` subclass that adds an `addInterest(rate)` method.

questions.question: A `<script type="module">` is deferred automatically, so it runs after the HTML has been parsed.
questions.explanation: Module scripts behave as if they had the defer attribute: they are fetched in parallel and executed after parsing, in document order.

questions.question: Inside the constructor of `class Dog extends Animal`, what does `super(name)` do?
questions.explanation: super(...) calls the parent class constructor, which creates and initialises the object. It must run before this is used in the subclass constructor.
